pos: n. (James Petigru Boyce, 1827–1888, founder and first president of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary and author of the Abstract of Systematic Theology)
etymology: Hebrew Yaaqob, supplanter; Petigru, a family name of Huguenot origin; Norman French Boyce, a wood.
biblical_def: James Petigru Boyce was the son of one of the richest men in Charleston. He studied at Brown University under Francis Wayland, was converted in 1846, and went on to Princeton Theological Seminary, where Charles Hodge's Reformed theology shaped him for life. In 1856, as a young professor at Furman University, he gave an inaugural address on Three Changes in Theological Institutions, proposing a common seminary for Southern Baptists that would train men of every level of education and would require every professor to sign a confession of faith, so that the churches could hold their teachers accountable. The Southern Baptist Theological Seminary opened at Greenville, South Carolina, in 1859, with Boyce, John Broadus, Basil Manly Jr., and William Williams as its faculty and Manly's Abstract of Principles as its confession. Boyce kept the school alive through the Civil War and Reconstruction, spent much of his own fortune on it, and moved it to Louisville in 1877. In 1879 he required the resignation of Crawford Toy, a gifted professor who had adopted critical views of Scripture's inspiration, and grieved over it. His Abstract of Systematic Theology (1887) is a clear Calvinistic theology for preachers. His aim was that the church be “the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education, and theology as the science of God and divine things.
webster_full: SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed.
THEOL'OGY, n. Divinity; the science of God and divine things.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. Consent or attestation given by underwriting the name.
scriptures: But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.
If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: The founder who bound Southern Seminary's professors to a confession, and enforced it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Boyce's central insight is the one Southern Baptists forgot for most of the twentieth century and recovered at great cost: that a theological school will drift unless its teachers are bound to a confession and the binding is enforced. Paul's charge to Timothy is a charge to every faculty: “That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost” (2Ti 1:14).

The Toy case shows the cost. Boyce loved Toy and grieved to lose him, but a professor who taught that Scripture erred could not keep his chair, because “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21). The honest caveat is that Boyce, like most of the founders, was a slaveholder and defended the Confederacy, which the dictionary names as a grave moral failure the seminary has rightly confessed.

roots_lines: Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, wholesome; 1 Timothy 6:3.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, move; 2 Peter 1:21.
usage: “the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) — the church a seminary serves.
“That good thing which was committed unto thee keep” (2Ti 1:14) — the case for confessional subscription.
“If any man teach otherwise” (1Ti 6:3) — the Toy resignation.

pos: n. (John Albert Broadus, 1827–1895, founding professor and second president of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary and author of On the Preparation and Delivery of Sermons)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Broadus, a Virginia family name.
biblical_def: John Albert Broadus was a Virginian, a master of Greek at the University of Virginia, and pastor of the Baptist church at Charlottesville when Boyce persuaded him to join the founding faculty of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary in 1859, to teach New Testament and preaching. He spent the Civil War as a chaplain in Lee's army. When the seminary reopened in 1865 almost without students, Broadus delivered his full course of lectures on homiletics to a single blind student, and those lectures, revised and published in 1870 as A Treatise on the Preparation and Delivery of Sermons, became the most widely used textbook on preaching in America for a century. His Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew (1886) is a model of careful, reverent exegesis, and his Harmony of the Gospels served generations of students. He succeeded Boyce as president in 1889. Broadus held that the preacher's task is to explain the text, apply it, and press it on the hearer's conscience, in plain language and with real feeling, because God has chosen preaching as His means of saving sinners: “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21). His homiletic was Ezra's Levites: “they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense” (Neh 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines homiletics as the art of preaching, and a treatise as a written composition on a particular subject.
webster_full: HOMILET'ICS, n. The art of preaching.
TREA'TISE, n. A tract; a written composition on a particular subject, in which the principles of it are discussed or explained.
SER'MON, n. A discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergyman, for the purpose of religious instruction.
scriptures: For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
corruption_summary: The preaching professor who lectured a full course to one blind student and taught a century of preachers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Broadus's homiletic stands against the modern sermon that begins with the listener's felt needs and finds a text to suit them. For Broadus the text governs: the preacher's first duty is to find what the passage means, and only then to apply it. Paul's charge is the method: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

The honest caveat is the one his generation shares: Broadus served as a Confederate chaplain and defended the society that held slaves, which the dictionary names as a failure. The principle to recover from his best work is the aim Paul gave preaching, “warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Col 1:28).
roots_lines: Hebrew parash (H6567) — to make distinct, read distinctly; Nehemiah 8:8.
usage: “by the foolishness of preaching” (1Co 1:21) — why homiletics matters.
“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — the expository method.
“present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Col 1:28) — the aim of the sermon.

pos: n. (Basil Manly Jr., 1825–1892, Southern Baptist educator, author of the Abstract of Principles and of The Bible Doctrine of Inspiration)
etymology: Greek Basileios, kingly; English Manly, from a place-name.
biblical_def: Basil Manly Jr. was the son of Basil Manly Sr., pastor at Charleston and president of the University of Alabama. Educated at the University of Alabama, Newton Theological Institution, and Princeton Seminary, he served as a pastor in Alabama and Virginia and as principal of the Richmond Female Institute before joining Boyce and Broadus on the founding faculty of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary in 1859, where he taught Old Testament. In 1858 he drafted the seminary's confession, the Abstract of Principles. He was the first president of the Sunday School Board of the Southern Baptist Convention in 1863, president of Georgetown College in Kentucky in the 1870s, and a hymn-writer and compiler of hymnals, including Baptist Psalmody with his father; his hymn Soldiers of Christ, in Truth Arrayed is still sung at the seminary's commencement. His book The Bible Doctrine of Inspiration (1888), written in the wake of the Toy controversy, defended the full verbal inspiration of Scripture against the critical theories then entering American seminaries. His conviction was the psalmist's: “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7), and the apostle's, that “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inspiration as the supernatural influence of the Spirit of God on the human mind, by which prophets and apostles were qualified to set forth divine truth.
webster_full: INSPIRA'TION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit; the supernatural influence of the Spirit of God on the human mind, by which prophets, apostles and sacred writers were qualified to set forth divine truth without any mixture of error.
HYMNOL'OGY, n. A collection of hymns.
AB'STRACT, n. A summary or epitome, containing the substance, a general view, or the principal heads of a treatise or writing.
scriptures: Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
corruption_summary: The author of Southern Seminary's confession and a defense of verbal inspiration.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the critical theory of Scripture Manly answered as a corruption of the doctrine of inspiration: the view, then arriving from German universities, that the Bible contains the word of God mixed with human error, so that the scholar must sift the one from the other. Paul's claim is wider: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), every part of it.

The principle to recover is Manly's pairing of confession and song. The man who wrote the seminary's doctrinal standard also wrote its hymn, because truth confessed should be truth sung, “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19). His generation's defence of slavery is a failure the dictionary names; his defence of Scripture is a legacy to keep.
roots_summary: Hebrew tamim (H8549), perfect; shub (H7725), to convert; Greek theopneustos (G2315), inspired.
roots_lines: Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, restore, convert; Psalm 19:7.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear along, move; 2 Peter 1:21.
usage: “The law of the LORD is perfect” (Psa 19:7) — the doctrine of inspiration in a line.
“moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — how Scripture was given.
“in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19) — the hymn-writer's warrant.

pos: n. (the twenty-article confession of faith written by Basil Manly Jr. in 1858 for the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary)
etymology: Latin abstractus, drawn off, a summary; principium, a beginning, foundation.
biblical_def: The Abstract of Principles is the confession of faith of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, drafted by Basil Manly Jr. at the request of the founders and adopted in 1858. It consists of twenty short articles drawn largely from the Second London Confession as it had been received in the Philadelphia and Charleston associations: on the Scriptures, God, the Trinity, providence, election, the fall of man, the Mediator, regeneration, repentance, faith, justification, sanctification, perseverance of the saints, the church, baptism, the Lord's Supper, the Lord's Day, liberty of conscience, the resurrection, and the judgment. Its doctrine of grace is plainly Calvinistic: election is God's eternal choice of some persons unto everlasting life, not because of foreseen merit in them; regeneration is a change of heart wrought by the Holy Spirit; and those whom God has accepted in the Beloved shall never totally nor finally fall away. Boyce insisted that every professor sign it, promising to teach in accordance with and not contrary to it, and that any departure be grounds for resignation. The seminary drifted from it in the twentieth century while still requiring the signature, and recovered it after 1993. Its purpose was Paul's: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a principle as a fundamental truth, a tenet, and an abstract as a summary containing the substance.
webster_full: PRIN'CIPLE, n. Ground; foundation; that which supports an assertion, an action, or a series of actions or of reasoning; a tenet, that which is believed.
AB'STRACT, n. A summary or epitome, containing the substance, a general view, or the principal heads of a treatise or writing.
ARTICLE, n. A point of faith; a doctrinal point or proposition in theology.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Southern Seminary's Calvinistic confession, signed for a century by men who no longer held it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Abstract's history is a parable of confessional subscription. For much of the twentieth century professors signed a confession of unconditional election and the perseverance of the saints while teaching that Scripture erred and that election was a matter of human choice. A signature that binds no one has become what Paul warned against, consenting in form while one “consent not to wholesome words” (1Ti 6:3).

The principle to recover is the one the Abstract's recovery after 1993 demonstrated: a confession can be restored when trustees insist that it means what it says. Its article on election stands on Eph 1:4, “he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4), and it was written to be believed.
roots_summary: Greek hupotuposis (G5296), form, pattern; hugiaino (G5198), to be sound; eklegomai (G1586), to choose.
roots_lines: Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Greek proserchomai (G4334) — to come to, consent to; 1 Timothy 6:3.
usage: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — why the founders wrote it.
“he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4) — the article on election.
“consent not to wholesome words” (1Ti 6:3) — the drift of the twentieth century.

pos: n. (Annie Walker Armstrong, 1850–1938, of Baltimore, first corresponding secretary of the Woman's Missionary Union of the Southern Baptist Convention)
etymology: Hebrew Channah, grace; English Armstrong, strong in the arm.
biblical_def: Annie Armstrong was born into a prosperous Baptist family in Baltimore, was converted as a young woman, and was for most of her life a member of the city's Eutaw Place Baptist Church. She gave her life to missions without ever going to the field. In Baltimore she organized mission work among the poor, immigrants, and freed slaves, and in 1888 she led in organizing the Woman's Missionary Union, auxiliary to the Southern Baptist Convention, serving as its first corresponding secretary until 1906. She refused any salary. By an enormous correspondence — she is said to have written some eighteen thousand letters in a single year — she linked the women of Southern Baptist churches to missionaries at home and abroad, organized societies in every state, and gathered gifts of money, clothing, and supplies. When Lottie Moon wrote from China in 1887 urging Southern Baptist women to give a special Christmas offering for missions, Armstrong organized the first such offering in 1888. The annual Easter offering for home missions was named for her in 1934. Her model was the women of the Gospels who “ministered unto him of their substance” (Luk 8:3), and her prayer was Christ's: “Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Mat 9:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion, and an auxiliary as a helper or assistant.
webster_full: MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion.
AUXIL'IARY, n. A helper; an assistant; a confederate in some action or enterprise.
CORRESPOND'ENCE, n. Intercourse between persons at a distance, by means of letters sent and answers received.
scriptures: Luk 8:3
And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
Rom 16:1
I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:
And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:
corruption_summary: A Baltimore laywoman who organized Southern Baptist women to pray for and support missions.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Armstrong is sometimes enlisted in arguments for women's ordination. The record will not bear it. She organized women to serve the missionary work of the churches as an auxiliary, under the Convention, and the women she rallied are in the biblical line of Phebe, “a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea” (Rom 16:1), and of the women Paul thanked for labouring with him in the gospel.

The principle to recover is the dignity of unseen service. A woman who never preached a sermon or crossed an ocean did more for missions than most who did, by prayer, letters, and the gathering of gifts. Christ's praise of the widow's mite is the measure: “this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury” (Mar 12:43).
usage: “ministered unto him of their substance” (Luk 8:3) — the Woman's Missionary Union.
“Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest” (Mat 9:38) — the first duty of a mission society.
“this poor widow hath cast more in” (Mar 12:43) — the Christmas offering of 1888.

pos: n. (the General Missionary Convention of the Baptist Denomination in the United States, formed in 1814 and meeting every three years, divided in 1845)
etymology: Latin triennium, a period of three years; conventio, a coming together.
biblical_def: The Triennial Convention was the first national body of American Baptists. When Adoniram and Ann Judson and Luther Rice, sent to India in 1812 by the Congregationalist American Board, became convinced on the voyage that believer's baptism is the teaching of Scripture and were immersed in Calcutta, they resigned from the Board, and Rice returned to America to rally Baptist support. In May 1814, delegates from Baptist societies and churches met in Philadelphia and formed the General Missionary Convention of the Baptist Denomination in the United States of America for Foreign Missions, called the Triennial Convention from its schedule of meetings. Richard Furman of Charleston was its first president, and it adopted the Judsons in Burma as its missionaries. Under Rice's influence it also took up home missions and education and founded Columbian College in Washington. In 1844, asked whether it would appoint a slaveholder as a missionary, its board replied that it would not; Baptists of the South withdrew, and in May 1845 at Augusta, Georgia, they formed the Southern Baptist Convention. The Triennial Convention's founding text was the Great Commission: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a convention as an assembly of delegates for consultation on important concerns.
webster_full: CONVEN'TION, n. An assembly of delegates or representatives for consultation on important concerns, civil, political or ecclesiastical.
TRIEN'NIAL, a. Continuing three years; happening every three years.
DEL'EGATE, n. A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Act 13:2
As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.
Act 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
corruption_summary: The first national Baptist missionary body, formed for Burma and divided over slavery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Triennial Convention was formed because two missionaries became Baptists on a ship, and its founders saw in that providence a call: “how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15). Baptists who had been scattered and suspicious of one another found in missions a reason to unite.

Its division is the shadow on its history. The dictionary names the defence of slaveholding that led Southern Baptists to separate in 1845 as sin, as the Southern Baptist Convention itself confessed in 1995. The principle to recover is that cooperation in missions must rest on agreement in the gospel and its ethics, and that the missionary call of Act 16:9, “Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Act 16:9), is not served by churches that hold their own brethren in bondage.
roots_summary: Greek matheteuo (G3100), to teach, make disciples; apostello (G649), to send; aphorizo (G873), to separate.
roots_lines: Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to make disciples, teach; Matthew 28:19.
Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, set apart; Acts 13:2.
usage: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) — the convention's charter.
“how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15) — why Baptists organized.
“Separate me Barnabas and Saul” (Act 13:2) — the sending church.

pos: n. (Luther Rice, 1783–1836, missionary to India who became a Baptist and returned to organize American Baptists for missions)
etymology: German Luther, from liut, people, and heri, army; English Rice, from Welsh Rhys, ardour.
biblical_def: Luther Rice was a Massachusetts Congregationalist who studied at Williams College and Andover Seminary and joined the circle of students, with Adoniram Judson and Samuel Mills, who pledged themselves to foreign missions. In February 1812 he was ordained with Judson and others as a missionary of the American Board and sailed for India on a different ship. Like the Judsons, he studied the question of baptism on the voyage and in Calcutta, became persuaded that the New Testament teaches the baptism of believers only, and was immersed by William Ward of the Serampore mission in November 1812. Because the Judsons could not be supported by the Congregationalists, Rice returned to America in 1813 to seek support among Baptists, travelling thousands of miles on horseback, preaching, and forming missionary societies. His work led to the formation of the Triennial Convention in 1814, which he served as agent for the rest of his life. He also founded the Baptist newspaper the Columbian Star and Columbian College in Washington, whose debts clouded his later years. He never married and never returned to the field. He obeyed Paul's pattern: “I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision” (Act 26:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an agent as one entrusted with the business of another, and immersion as the act of putting into a fluid below the surface.
webster_full: A'GENT, n. One entrusted with the business of another; a substitute; a deputy.
IMMER'SION, n. The act of putting into a fluid below the surface; baptism by plunging the whole body.
MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion.
scriptures: Whereupon, O king Agrippa, I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision:
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation:
corruption_summary: The missionary who came home to make American Baptists a missionary people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Rice's life is a reminder that the missionary enterprise requires those who go and those who send, and that the second calling is no less a calling. He wanted to return to India and never could, because the churches needed someone to make them see the field. The prophet's praise belongs to both: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7).

The honest caveat is Columbian College, a worthy aim pursued with more zeal than prudence, whose debts brought charges of mismanagement against him. The principle to recover is the one Paul held in his own planning: the gospel must go “not where Christ was named” (Rom 15:20), and every institution at home is measured by whether it sends.
roots_summary: Greek apeithes (G545), disobedient; optasia (G3701), vision; Hebrew basar (H1319), to bring good tidings.
roots_lines: Greek euangelizo (G2097) — to bring good news; Romans 10:15.
usage: “I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision” (Act 26:19) — Calcutta, 1812.
“how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15) — his message to the churches.
“not where Christ was named” (Rom 15:20) — the aim of missions.

pos: n. (John Leland, 1754–1841, Baptist preacher in Virginia and Massachusetts and advocate of religious liberty)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Leland, fallow land.
biblical_def: John Leland was born in Massachusetts, converted in 1772, and spent fifteen years from 1776 as an itinerant Baptist preacher in Virginia, where Baptists had been jailed and beaten for preaching without licence. He baptized hundreds and became the leading voice of Virginia Baptists in their struggle against the established Episcopal Church and its tax. In 1788 he was a candidate to Virginia's convention to ratify the federal Constitution, opposed because it lacked a guarantee of religious liberty; by tradition he met James Madison and withdrew in Madison's favour on his assurance that such an amendment would be pursued, and the First Amendment followed. In 1791 he returned to Massachusetts, settled at Cheshire, and published The Rights of Conscience Inalienable, arguing that government has no jurisdiction over religion and that every man must give account of himself to God. In 1802 his congregation sent President Jefferson a cheese of over twelve hundred pounds. Leland was also suspicious of confessions of faith, missionary societies, and theological education, which he feared would become new establishments, and this restlessness weakened the churches he loved. His principle was Paul's: “every one of us shall give account of himself to God” (Rom 14:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conscience as internal or self-knowledge, the faculty that decides on the lawfulness of our own actions.
webster_full: CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty, power or principle within us, which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our own actions.
INALIEN'ABLE, a. That cannot be legally or justly alienated or transferred to another.
ITIN'ERANT, a. Wandering; not settled; passing or travelling from place to place.
scriptures: So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Gal 5:13
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
corruption_summary: A Virginia Baptist who pressed for religious liberty and distrusted every human institution, confessions included.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Leland is the patron of the modern notion that faith is a purely private matter between the individual and God, but the notion goes beyond him. He held that the state has no jurisdiction over worship because Christ does, and that men answer to God, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). His liberty was liberty to obey Christ, not liberty from Him.

The honest caveat is his individualism in the church. Suspicion of confessions and associations as new establishments mistakes the liberty Paul defends, which is “not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13), and which binds believers to one another in a shared faith. Baptists who kept Leland's view of the state and dropped his view of the church were the wiser.
roots_lines: Greek logos (G3056) — a word, an account; Romans 14:12.
Greek aphorme (G874) — a starting point, occasion; Galatians 5:13.
usage: “every one of us shall give account of himself to God” (Rom 14:12) — the rights of conscience.
“unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21) — the limit of the state.
“by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13) — the limit of individualism.

pos: n. (Shubal Stearns, 1706–1771, New England Separate Baptist who founded the Sandy Creek church in North Carolina in 1755)
etymology: Hebrew Shubael, captive of God; English Stearns, from stern, severe.
biblical_def: Shubal Stearns was born in Boston, converted under the preaching of George Whitefield in 1745 during the Great Awakening, and joined the New Light Separates who left the established Congregational churches. In 1751 he became convinced of believer's baptism and was baptized. In 1754, believing God was calling him westward, he set out with his family and that of his brother-in-law Daniel Marshall, and in 1755 they settled at Sandy Creek in Guilford County, North Carolina, a raw frontier settlement. There a church of sixteen members grew within a few years to over six hundred. Stearns was a small man with a piercing eye and a voice of remarkable power, whose preaching produced weeping, trembling, and conversions across the Carolina backcountry. In 1758 the Sandy Creek Association was formed, and by Morgan Edwards's reckoning, within seventeen years the movement had planted forty-two churches and raised up a hundred and twenty-five ministers from Virginia to Georgia. Stearns's Separate Baptists were the seed of much of the later Baptist South. The growth was the Lord's, as in Antioch: “the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord” (Act 11:21).

FRON'TIER, n. The marches; the border, confine, or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
REVI'VAL, n. Renewed and more active attention to religion; an awakening of men to their spiritual concerns.

corruption_summary: A Whitefield convert whose frontier church at Sandy Creek mothered the Baptist South.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Stearns's story is often told as a lesson in revival technique, as though his methods produced the growth. His hearers would have said the opposite: God made a people willing, “Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power” (Psa 110:3), and “the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved” (Act 2:47).

The honest caveat concerns the Separate Baptists' practice, which carried enthusiasm into disorder at times, as the next entry notes. The principle to recover is the frontier preacher's urgency joined to dependence on God alone for the fruit.

pos: n. (the Baptists who arose from the New Light Separates of the Great Awakening, especially in the South after 1755)
etymology: Latin separatus, set apart; Greek baptistes, one who baptizes.
biblical_def: The Separate Baptists were the Baptist fruit of the Great Awakening. In New England, many converts of the revivals left the established Congregational churches as New Light Separates, and some of these, studying the question of baptism, became Baptists. Shubal Stearns and Daniel Marshall carried the movement to North Carolina in 1755, and from the Sandy Creek church and association it spread with great speed through Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia. Separate Baptists were known for fervent, emotional preaching, for lay exhorters, for intense opposition from the established Anglican clergy and magistrates, and for refusing at first to adopt any written confession, fearing it would quench the Spirit. Morgan Edwards recorded that they practised nine rites: baptism, the Lord's Supper, love feasts, laying on of hands, washing of feet, anointing the sick, the right hand of fellowship, the kiss of charity, and the devoting of children; and that they allowed women to act as eldresses and exhort publicly. Their relations with the confessional Regular Baptists were at first cool, but they united in Virginia in 1787 and in Kentucky in 1801 as United Baptists, on the understanding that the Philadelphia Confession be received without being imposed in every particular. Their growth was the Lord's doing: “the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved” (Act 2:47).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a separatist as one who withdraws from an established church, and an exhorter as one who encourages by words.
webster_full: SEP'ARATIST, n. One that withdraws from a church, or that dissents from an established church.
EXHORT'ER, n. One who exhorts or encourages; in some churches, one who is licensed to exhort but not to preach.
BAP'TIST, n. One who administers baptism; one who denies the doctrine of infant baptism and maintains that baptism ought to be administered only to adults by immersion.

corruption_summary: Awakening Baptists of the Southern frontier, fervent and fruitful, and loose at first in order.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names one Separate Baptist practice as departure from apostolic order: the appointment of eldresses and the public exhortation of women in the assembly, which Paul forbids, “Let your women keep silence in the churches” (1Co 14:34). The ordinances they multiplied from Joh 13:14, “ye also ought to wash one another's feet” (Joh 13:14), and from the kiss of Rom 16:16 confused examples of humility and affection with commanded ordinances of worship.

The honest record is mostly praise. They preached Christ to the frontier with a fervour the settled churches lacked, suffered jail and violence for it in Virginia, and helped win religious liberty for the nation. The principle to recover is the one their union with the Regular Baptists embodied: fire and order belong together, and the confession that guards the doctrine does not quench the Spirit who inspired it.
